name: WILLIS LEASE FINANCE

priced.reason: not a repriceable fcff name or no growth supplied

devils_advocate.strongest_counter: The strongest case that I am wrong is that net fleet investment, not gross, is the right charge: Willis routinely trades engines, and in the six months to 2026-06-30 it sold $302.8M of equipment against $401.9M of purchases, so net fleet investment was only $99.1M and in H1 2025 only $13.0M. On that reading free cash flow is real and the $347.6M base is not absurd. A second counter is that an engine lessor is economically a financial: the right frame is return on tangible book, and at ~12x earnings with AUM compounding 21% the name is not obviously expensive, so calling the DCF broken does not by itself make the stock rich.
devils_advocate.what_would_prove_it: A full-year cash flow statement showing CFO less NET fleet investment consistently at or near the $250-350M the model assumes, sustained across a cycle rather than in a year with unusually heavy engine sales.
devils_advocate.already_visible: Partly, and it cuts against the model rather than for it. H1 2026: CFO $134.2M less net fleet investment $99.1M = $35.1M, and after $42.5M of notes-receivable issuance and $39.6M of JV contributions, cash used in investing was $78.2M against CFO of $134.2M. H1 2025 was better ($132.2M on the same basis) but that was a year with almost no fleet growth. Neither half-year supports $347.6M annualised, and the equipment portfolio is $2,783.4M against a D&A charge that implies well over $200M of annual sustaining reinvestment.
devils_advocate.unresolved: I could not determine the split between growth and maintenance fleet capex, which is the number that decides the true owner-earnings base. Willis does not disclose it and it cannot be derived from the tags.

what_changed: Closed a portfolio acquisition of 12 aircraft and 13 engines on 2026-08-25 (8-K item 2.01), after the 2026-06-30 balance sheet the model prices. Announced a new Willis Engine Repair Center in Malaysia (2026-08-27). Q2 earnings fell year over year on lower maintenance reserve revenue and higher G&A and technical expense. Further 8-Ks on 2026-07-14 (item 1.01) and 2026-09-08. PRIOR RESEARCH: this name was last covered on 2026-08-31, which reached the same no_model verdict and diagnosed the capex defect correctly from the committed extract, but recorded two things it could not settle — "I could not read the 10-K to state the correct equipment-purchase figure" and "I could not read the 2026-08-25 item 2.01 8-K". Both are now closed by dispatching adhoc-fetch: the purchase line is $401,934k for H1 2026 against $6,287k of furnishings capex, and the 2026-08-25 8-K is a portfolio acquisition of 12 aircraft and 13 engines. I agree with that pass and it was right to cap itself; the only correction is that its corrected base was guessed at "plausibly negative" whereas the actual H1 figures give $35.1M of CFO less net fleet investment, i.e. small and positive, not negative. One defect it raised has since been FIXED: it reported a fabricated -69.7% 63-day move caused by the 3-for-1 split of 2026-07-17 not being applied to the pre-split price series; today's brief shows 63d -7.0% and 252d +16.7%, which are plausible, so the split adjustment is now working and the beta of 1.32 (R-squared 0.243) is no longer computed on a corrupted series.
consensus_case: Willis Lease is a leveraged aircraft-engine lessor in the best engine-leasing market in twenty years: AUM up 21% year over year to $4.4 billion, Q2 2026 revenue $194M, pre-tax income $38.1M, adjusted EBITDA $120.7M, and diluted EPS of $2.39 for the first half. Spare CFM56 and V2500 capacity is scarce because GTF and LEAP shop visits are keeping narrowbodies grounded, so lease rates and maintenance reserves are firm. At $57.43 the equity is roughly 12x annualised first-half EPS. The market is paying a normal multiple for a levered, cyclical asset owner whose earnings are real but whose growth requires continuously buying more engines with borrowed money.
base_case_rationale: I cannot state a defensible five-year FCFF growth rate because the FCFF base this model is built on does not describe the company. See fcff_base_override and the data-quality note: the capex the extractor can see is office furniture, not engines.
key_risks: Engine values and lease rates are at a cyclical high driven by GTF/LEAP durability problems; a resolution of those programmes releases spare capacity and compresses both
66% debt weight in the capital structure against a WACC the engine computes at 13.9% - refinancing risk if credit spreads widen
Consolidation of AUM into managed vehicles makes reported revenue and asset growth harder to tie back to equity value
watch_for: A full-year 2026 cash flow statement showing purchases of equipment held for operating lease against proceeds from sale of equipment - the two lines that decide whether any free cash flow exists
Disclosure separating growth from maintenance fleet investment
Any narrowing of the GTF/LEAP shop-visit backlog, which is the demand driver for the whole spare-engine market
